questions.question: How many faces does a rectangular prism (a box) have?
questions.explain: A rectangular prism has 6 faces: top, bottom, front, back, left, and right. A common mistake is counting only the 3 or 4 faces you can see at a glance and forgetting the hidden ones.

questions.question: A single unit cube sits on a flat table. How many squares appear in the front view?
questions.explain: Looking straight at the front of one cube, you see exactly one face — a single square. The top and side faces are not part of the front view, so you should not count them.

questions.question: A net consists of 2 triangles and 3 rectangles. When folded, it forms:
questions.explain: A triangular prism has exactly 2 triangular ends and 3 rectangular sides. A cube uses 6 squares, a cone uses a circle and a sector, and a rectangular prism uses 6 rectangles.

questions.question: A student is cutting wooden panels for an open-top bentwood box (no lid). The box is 30 cm long × 20 cm wide × 15 cm tall. How many rectangular panels does she need for the complete net?
questions.explain: An open-top box has a bottom panel plus 4 side panels, giving 5 rectangles total. The trap is counting 6 (as if it were a closed box) or 4 (forgetting the bottom).

questions.question: A 3D object is made of 4 unit cubes: three in a left-to-right row on the floor, with a fourth stacked directly on the middle one. In the side view (looking from the left), how many squares are visible?
questions.explain: From the left, all cubes share the same depth, so they overlap in the view. You only see the height profile: one square at the bottom and one on top, giving 2. The trap is counting each cube separately (3 or 4).

questions.question: A lidded basket has an open rectangular body (5 faces: bottom and 4 sides) plus a flat rectangular lid (1 face). How many rectangles appear in the complete net?
questions.explain: The open body contributes 5 rectangles and the lid adds 1, for 6 total. Students often write 7 by accidentally adding a phantom face, or 5 by forgetting the lid entirely.

questions.question: A closed-box net has 6 rectangles: two are 10 cm × 5 cm, two are 10 cm × 8 cm, and two are 8 cm × 5 cm. What are the three dimensions of the box?
questions.explain: Each matching pair of rectangles is a set of opposite faces, so the three distinct sizes (10, 8, 5) are the length, width, and height. The trap is reading a shared number like 10 as appearing twice in the dimensions.

questions.question: A rectangular block (20 cm long × 10 cm deep × 5 cm tall) sits on a desk. Its front view is a 20 cm wide × 5 cm tall rectangle. The block is then rotated 90° clockwise around its vertical axis. What are the dimensions of the new front view?
questions.explain: A 90° rotation swaps which horizontal dimension faces you (20 cm becomes 10 cm), but the height (5 cm) never changes. The trap is thinking the height becomes 10 cm or that the original 20 cm width stays.

questions.question: A student claims a closed rectangular box net only needs 5 rectangles because 'one face is hidden behind the others.' A classmate disagrees. What is the correct understanding?
options: The classmate is right: a closed box has 6 faces, so the net must include all 6 rectangles.
The student is right: the back face is invisible in the front view, so it is not part of the net.
The classmate is right, but only 4 panels are needed if the box is a square prism.
The student is right: opposite faces are identical, so one pair can be omitted.
questions.explain: A closed rectangular prism has 6 faces, and every face needs a panel in the net to fold into a solid box. 'Hidden in a 2-D view' does not mean 'does not exist in 3-D.' This is the most common error when moving from views to nets.

questions.question: A student builds a 3D object: a 3 × 2 base of unit cubes (6 cubes) plus 2 extra cubes stacked on the back-left and back-right positions. In the front view, how many squares are visible?
questions.explain: In the front view the back-row base cubes are hidden behind the front-row cubes, but the two raised cubes (second layer) peek above and are visible. You see 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 squares, not all 8 cubes. The trap is simply counting every cube in the object.

questions.question: A student builds a 2 × 2 × 2 cube (8 unit cubes) and removes the front-top-right cube. Her friend says the front view is now an L-shape of 3 squares. Is the friend correct?
options: No — the front view is still a full 2 × 2 square because the cube behind fills the gap.
Yes — removing one cube always removes one square from the front view.
No — the front view now shows only 1 square.
Yes — the front view is a 2 × 2 square with the top-right missing, showing 3 squares.
questions.explain: In a 2 × 2 × 2 cube every front-facing position has a cube directly behind it. Removing the front-top-right cube simply reveals the back-top-right cube's front face, so the front view is unchanged. The trap is assuming a removed cube always creates a visible gap in the view.

questions.question: A can of soup stands upright on the kitchen counter. Which shape do you see in the top view (looking straight down at it)?
questions.explain: Looking straight down at an upright can, you see the flat round lid, so the top view is a circle; the answer that says rectangle is the trap because that is the front view of the can, not the top view.

questions.question: A net is made of 6 identical squares joined edge to edge. When it is folded up, which 3D object does it make?
options: A rectangular prism that is not a cube
questions.explain: Six faces that are all the same square means every edge has the same length, so it folds into a cube; the answer about a rectangular prism that is not a cube is the common trap, since that shape needs faces of different sizes, not 6 identical squares.

questions.question: Two unit cubes sit side by side in a left-to-right row on a desk. How many squares are visible in the top view (looking straight down)?
questions.explain: From above you see the top face of each cube, and there are 2 cubes side by side, so the top view is 2 squares in a row; the answer that says 4 is the trap of counting faces you cannot see from above instead of just the top faces.

questions.question: Which set of shapes forms the net of a square-based pyramid?
questions.explain: A square-based pyramid has one square base plus one triangle folding up from each of the base's 4 edges, so the net is 1 square and 4 triangles; the answer that says 1 square and 3 triangles is the trap of forgetting that a square base has 4 edges, not 3.
